prompt.en: An SSB processor raises average output while the transmitter is already at its clean peak limit. Which operating decision follows?

text.en: Increase drive until the peak reading rises as much as the average reading.

feedback.en: The clean peak limit is already reached. More drive can cause clipping and unwanted bandwidth.

text.en: Reduce processing or drive as needed to keep peaks within the clean limit.

feedback.en: A higher average reading does not justify exceeding the peak limit or losing clean operation.

text.en: Treat a higher average reading as proof that the peak limit has increased.

feedback.en: Processing changes the distribution of signal levels, not the transmitter's allowed clean peak.

text.en: Judge the setting by the average meter alone because processed speech has no separate peak limit.

feedback.en: Processing does not remove peak limits. Both the envelope peaks and the transmitted quality still matter.

explanation.en: Average power and peak envelope power are different. Processing cannot create extra clean peak headroom.

prompt.en: Two packet links detect damaged frames. Link A records an error and moves on. Link B requests a repeat until a check passes or retries run out. Which suits a form that must arrive intact or be reported as failed?

text.en: Link A, because detecting the error makes a damaged frame usable without a repeat.

feedback.en: Detecting damage identifies a problem. It does not supply the missing or corrupted information.

text.en: Link B, because it can replace damaged data with a checked copy or report failure.

feedback.en: Repeat requests can obtain a clean copy within a retry limit. Failure can be reported rather than silently keeping damaged data.

text.en: Either link, because both have already corrected the frame by checking it.

feedback.en: An error check alone is detection, not reconstruction of the original content. The repeat supplies a new copy.

text.en: Link A, because fewer transmissions give stronger evidence that every field arrived.

feedback.en: Fewer transmissions may be faster, but speed does not verify delivery of each field.

explanation.en: ARQ adds a repeat-request exchange to error detection. It can obtain a verified copy or report that delivery failed within the retry limit.

prompt.en: A receiver shows a 2.5 kHz slice. Each trace is about 50 Hz wide, with 200 Hz total reserved for guard space. What is the closest count before practical spacing limits?

feedback.en: After the guard space, 2 300 Hz remains. Dividing by 100 Hz would give 23, but each stated trace is only 50 Hz wide.
This divides the full 2 500 Hz by 50 Hz without reserving the 200 Hz guard space.
Convert first: 2.5 kHz = 2 500 Hz. Then (2 500 - 200) / 50 = 46. Real operation also needs practical spacing.
This subtracts 200 Hz at each edge. The prompt reserves 200 Hz in total, so subtract it once.

explanation.en: Convert widths to the same unit, subtract the total reserved space, then divide. The result is a simple planning count, not a real channel allocation.
